Reprove
re-prūve´
v. (to charge with a fault, to convict; rendering Hebrew yakach, Greek elegcho)
From Latin reprobare, to disapprove, reject — the same root as reprobate. To reprove is to test a thing and find it wanting, then say so.

Biblical Definition

Reprove is to bring a fault home to a person, and Scripture treats it as an act of love rather than hostility. Abraham reproves Abimelech over a stolen well and the two make a covenant that same day (Gen 21:25) — reproof clearing the ground for peace rather than destroying it. The Chronicler records God Himself doing it on His people's behalf: “he reproved kings for their sakes” (1Ch 16:21). Job supplies the hard qualification that separates real reproof from mere argument: “How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?” (Job 6:25) — his friends had volume and had not touched him, because words only reprove when they are right. Job also warns the reprover that he is himself under scrutiny: “He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons” (Job 13:10). And Paul makes it a standing ministerial duty with a temperature attached: “reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines reprove as to blame, to censure, to charge with a fault to the face — and notes the sense of convincing of a fault, or proving it upon a person.

expand to see more

REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure.

I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices. Ps. l.

2. To charge with a fault to the face; to chide; to reprehend.

3. To blame for; with of; as, to reprove one of laziness. 4. To convince of a fault, or to make it manifest.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Job 6:25 — "How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?"

Gen 21:25 — "And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of a well of water, which Abimelech's servants had violently taken away."

Job 13:10 — "He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons."

Modern Corruption

Reproof reclassified as judgment or harm, so that the loving act Scripture commands is now the one act a friend may not perform — and, on the other side, harshness excused as faithfulness.

expand to see more

The reigning ethic makes acceptance the whole of love, and on that account reproof is an injury by definition. Scripture holds the opposite: faithful are the wounds of a friend, and it is the enemy's kisses that are deceitful. A friendship in which nothing may be said is not deeper than one in which it may; it is shallower, because it has been purchased by an agreement to leave each other alone. Proverbs makes reception of reproof the plainest test of wisdom there is — a reproof enters further into a wise man than a hundred stripes into a fool.

But Job 6:25 must be allowed its full weight against the reprovers. Job's friends were doctrinally confident, verbally fluent, and wrong, and he asks the devastating question: what doth your arguing reprove? Reproof that is not right words reproves nothing, however forcefully delivered. And Paul's command sets the manner along with the duty — with all longsuffering and doctrine — which excludes both the silence that will not speak and the impatience that speaks without teaching.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yakach (H3198), to decide, adjudge, reprove, correct — a legal root; Greek elegcho (G1651), to convict, expose, bring to light — the Spirit's own work in John 16:8.

expand to see more

Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to argue a case, adjudge, reprove; the same verb in come now, and let us reason together (Isa 1:18).

Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, refute, expose; the Comforter shall reprove the world of sin (John 16:8), so reproof is a work of the Spirit before it is a duty of men.

Greek epitimao (G2008) — to rebuke, censure sharply; distinguished from elegcho, which aims at conviction rather than mere censure.

Usage

"“Reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” — duty and manner together."

"“What doth your arguing reprove?” — fluency is not the same as right words."

"“He will surely reprove you, if ye do secretly accept persons” — the reprover is watched too."
